items.stem: The length of a table is 47 cm, correct to the nearest centimetre.

parts.t: Write down the lower bound of the length.
Write down the upper bound of the length.

sols: The measurement is correct to the nearest 1 cm, so the true length is within ½ × 1 = 0.5 cm of 47 cm.
half of the unit of accuracy
any length below 47.5 cm rounds down to 47 cm

items.stem: The mass of a parcel is 3.6 kg, correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.t: Write down the lower bound of the mass.
Write down the upper bound of the mass.

A number x is 8.40, correct to 2 decimal places.
Complete the error interval for x.
…………… ≤ x < ……………

sols: 1 decimal place means correct to the nearest 0.1 kg, so the half‑interval is 0.05 kg.
2 decimal places means correct to the nearest 0.01, so the half‑interval is 0.005.
the lower bound is included, the upper bound is not

items.stem:
A crate has a mass of 24 kg, correct to the nearest kilogram.
A lorry is loaded with 8 of these crates.

parts.t: Calculate the upper bound of the total mass of the 8 crates.
Calculate the lower bound of the total mass of the 8 crates.

sols: Each crate has upper bound 24 + 0.5 = 24.5 kg.
The total is largest when every crate is as heavy as possible.
Each crate has lower bound 24 − 0.5 = 23.5 kg.

items.stem:
The diagram shows a rectangle.
Its length is 12.4 cm and its width is 7.8 cm, each correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.t: Calculate the upper bound of the perimeter of the rectangle.

Calculate the upper bound of the area of the rectangle.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

sols: Upper bound of the length = 12.4 + 0.05 = 12.45 cm
Upper bound of the width = 7.8 + 0.05 = 7.85 cm
Upper bound of the perimeter = 40.6 cm
The area is largest when both sides take their upper bounds.
Upper bound of the area = 97.7 cm2 (3 s.f.)

items.stem:
A wooden plank has length 2.4 m, correct to 1 decimal place.
A piece of length 0.85 m, correct to 2 decimal places, is cut from the plank.

parts.t: Calculate the upper bound of the length of wood that is left.
Calculate the lower bound of the length of wood that is left.

sols: Plank: 2.35 ≤ length < 2.45. Piece cut off: 0.845 ≤ length < 0.855.
What is left is largest when the plank is longest and the piece cut off is shortest.
for a subtraction, use the upper bound minus the lower bound
What is left is smallest when the plank is shortest and the piece cut off is longest.

items.stem: A runner runs 480 m, correct to the nearest 10 m, in a time of 32.5 seconds, correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.t:
Calculate the upper bound of the runner's average speed.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

Calculate the lower bound of the runner's average speed.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

sols: Speed = distance ÷ time, so the speed is greatest when the distance is greatest and the time is least.
dividing by a smaller number gives a larger answer
The speed is least when the distance is least and the time is greatest.

items.stem:
A metal block has mass 250 g, correct to the nearest gram, and volume 62 cm3, correct to the nearest cubic centimetre.
The density of the block is found using density = mass ÷ volume.

parts.t:
Calculate the upper bound of the density.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

Calculate the lower bound of the density.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

sols: The density is greatest for the greatest mass and the smallest volume.
The density is least for the smallest mass and the greatest volume.

items.stem:
A cylinder has radius 4.5 cm, correct to 1 decimal place, and height 12 cm, correct to the nearest centimetre.
The volume of a cylinder is πr2h.

parts.t:
Calculate the upper bound of the volume of the cylinder.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

Calculate the lower bound of the volume of the cylinder.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

sols: Every factor is multiplied, so the volume is greatest when both are greatest.
The volume is least when both the radius and the height are least.
ms:
M1 for 4.55 and 12.5 both seen
M1 for π × 4.55² × 12.5
A1

items.stem:
The diagram shows a right-angled triangle.
The two shorter sides are 6.4 cm and 8.2 cm, each correct to 1 decimal place.
The hypotenuse has length h cm.

parts.t:
Calculate the upper bound of h.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

Calculate the lower bound of h.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

sols: The two shorter sides lie in 6.35 ≤ a < 6.45 and 8.15 ≤ b < 8.25.
h = √(a2 + b2), so h is greatest when both shorter sides are greatest.
h is least when both shorter sides are least.

M1 for 6.45 and 8.25 both seen

items.stem:
A cyclist travels 1480 m, correct to the nearest 10 m, in a time of 124.0 seconds, correct to the nearest 0.1 seconds.
The average speed of the cyclist is v m/s.

parts.t:
Calculate the upper bound of v.
Give your answer correct to 4 significant figures.

Calculate the lower bound of v.
Give your answer correct to 4 significant figures.

By comparing your answers to parts (a) and (b), write down the value of v to a suitable degree of accuracy.
Give a reason for your answer.

sols: The speed is greatest for the greatest distance and the least time.
The speed is least for the least distance and the greatest time.
Compare the two bounds digit by digit: 11.98… and 11.89…
To 3 significant figures they are 12.0 and 11.9 — these do not agree.
To 2 significant figures they are both 12.
the upper and lower bounds agree to 2 significant figures, so only 2 significant figures of the answer can be relied on
ms:
B1 for 12 (or 12 m/s)
B1 for a correct reason, e.g. both bounds round to 12 to 2 significant figures oe
FT their (a) and (b)

items.stem: The attendance at a football match is 12 000, correct to the nearest thousand.

parts.t: Write down the smallest possible attendance.
Write down the largest possible attendance.

sols: Correct to the nearest 1000 means the true value is within ½ × 1000 = 500 of 12 000.
half of the unit of accuracy
Attendance is a whole number of people, so the largest actual value is 12 499; the upper bound is 12 500
accept 12 499 as the largest whole number that rounds down
ms:
B1
accept 12 499 with a comment that the attendance is a whole number

items.stem: Each of these numbers is given correct to 2 significant figures.

parts.t:
a = 0.036
Complete the error interval for a.
…………… ≤ a < ……………

b = 5400
Complete the error interval for b.
…………… ≤ b < ……………

sols: The second significant figure of 0.036 is in the thousandths column, so the number is correct to the nearest 0.001 and the half‑interval is 0.0005.
The second significant figure of 5400 is the 4, in the hundreds column, so the number is correct to the nearest 100 and the half‑interval is 50.

items.stem: A kitchen scale weighs to the nearest 5 grams and a ruler measures to the nearest 0.5 cm.

parts.t:
A bar of chocolate weighs 85 g on the kitchen scale.
Write down the lower bound and the upper bound of the mass of the bar.

A pencil measures 12.5 cm on the ruler.
Complete the error interval for the length l cm of the pencil.
…………… ≤ l < ……………

sols: The unit of accuracy is 5 g, so the half‑interval is 2.5 g.
the bounds are half a unit either side, whatever the unit is
The unit of accuracy is 0.5 cm, so the half‑interval is 0.25 cm.

items.stem: The number of pupils in a school is 340, correct to the nearest 10.

parts.t: Write down the smallest possible number of pupils.
Write down the largest possible number of pupils.

sols: Correct to the nearest 10 means the number lies from 335 up to, but not including, 345.
335 rounds up to 340, so the smallest possible number = 335
The number of pupils is a whole number, so the largest value that is less than 345 is 344.
the upper bound 345 is not itself possible

parts.t: Write down the upper bound of the radius.

items.stem:
A rope is 12.6 m long, correct to 1 decimal place.
Pieces of length 0.45 m, correct to 2 decimal places, are cut from the rope.

parts.t:
Calculate the greatest number of pieces that can certainly be cut from the rope.
Show all your working.
Calculate the greatest number of pieces that could possibly be cut from the rope.

sols: To be certain, use the worst case: the shortest possible rope and the longest possible pieces.
lower bound ÷ upper bound gives the least number of pieces
Only whole pieces count, so 27 pieces can certainly be cut.
round down: a 28th piece might not be complete
The best case is the longest rope and the shortest pieces: 12.65 ÷ 0.445 = 28.42…
ms:
M1 for 12.55 and 0.455 seen
M1 for 12.55 ÷ 0.455 or 27.5…
A1 cao

items.stem:
A van can safely carry a load of up to 580 kg.
Each of 12 identical boxes has a mass of 48 kg, correct to the nearest kilogram.
Amir says: “12 × 48 = 576, so the van can safely carry all 12 boxes.”

parts.t: Explain, with a calculation, why Amir cannot be certain that he is right.

sols: Each box has upper bound 48 + 0.5 = 48.5 kg.
Upper bound of the total mass = 12 × 48.5 = 582 kg
582 kg is more than 580 kg, so the 12 boxes could weigh more than the safe load — Amir cannot be certain the van is safe.
the total is only guaranteed to lie between 12 × 47.5 = 570 kg and 582 kg
ms:
M1 for 48.5 seen
M1 for 12 × 48.5 = 582
A1 for a correct conclusion comparing 582 with 580

Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

Calculate the lower bound of the average speed of the tram, in km/h.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

sols: Speed is greatest for the greatest distance and the least time.
ms:

parts.t:
Calculate the upper bound of the length of a side of the tile.
Give your answer correct to 4 significant figures.

Calculate the lower bound of the length of a side of the tile.
Give your answer correct to 4 significant figures.

sols: Side = √A, and the square root is largest when the area is largest.
Upper bound of the side = 6.712 cm (4 s.f.)

parts.t: Calculate the upper bound of the area of the trapezium.
Calculate the lower bound of the area of the trapezium.

sols: half‑intervals of 0.05 cm, 0.05 cm and 0.5 cm
Area = ½(a + b)h — every quantity is added or multiplied, so the area is greatest when all three are greatest.

items.stem:
The acceleration a of a car is given by the formula  a = (v − u)⁄t.
u = 10 m/s and v = 24 m/s, each correct to the nearest 1 m/s.
t = 3.5 s, correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.t:
Calculate the upper bound of a.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

Calculate the lower bound of a.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

sols: v − u is greatest for the greatest v and the least u: 24.5 − 9.5 = 15.
for a subtraction use UB − LB

items.stem:
Rice costs $2.35 per kilogram.
A sack of rice has a mass of 5.0 kg, correct to the nearest 100 grams.

parts.t: Write down the lower bound of the mass of the sack.

Calculate the upper bound of the cost of the sack.
Give your answer correct to the nearest cent.

sols: 100 g = 0.1 kg, so the half‑interval is 0.05 kg.
Upper bound of the mass = 5.0 + 0.05 = 5.05 kg
The price per kilogram is exact, so the cost is greatest for the greatest mass.

items.stem:
The diagram shows a right-angled triangle.
The two shorter sides are 7.8 cm and 5.2 cm, each correct to 1 decimal place.
The angle marked θ is opposite the 5.2 cm side.

parts.t:
Calculate the upper bound of θ.
Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

Calculate the lower bound of θ.
Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

sols: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent, and tan increases as the angle increases, so θ is greatest when the fraction is greatest.
the given values 5.2 and 7.8 give 33.7°, which lies between the two bounds ✓
ms:
M1 for 5.25 and 7.75 seen
M1 for tan θ = 5.25⁄7.75 oe
A1

items.stem:
The diagram shows a triangle with two sides of length 9 cm and 12 cm, each correct to the nearest centimetre.
The angle between these two sides is 40°, correct to the nearest degree.

parts.t:
Calculate the upper bound of the area of the triangle.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

Calculate the lower bound of the area of the triangle.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

sols: Area = ½ab sin C. For an acute angle, sin C increases as C increases, so the area is greatest when a, b and C are all greatest.
the area rule; sin is increasing between 0° and 90°
Upper bound of the area = 38.6 cm2 (3 s.f.)
Lower bound of the area = 31.1 cm2 (3 s.f.)
ms:
B1 for 9.5, 12.5 and 40.5 seen
M1 for ½ × 9.5 × 12.5 × sin 40.5
A1

items.stem:
A cylindrical tin has a volume of 500 cm3, correct to the nearest 10 cm3, and a height of 8.0 cm, correct to 1 decimal place.
The volume of a cylinder is πr2h.

parts.t: Show that the upper bound of the radius of the tin is 4.50 cm, correct to 3 significant figures.

Calculate the lower bound of the radius of the tin.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

sols: Rearrange: r = √(V ÷ (πh)). The radius is greatest when V is greatest and h is least.
dividing by a smaller number gives a larger result
Upper bound of the radius = 4.50 cm (3 s.f.), as required
4.4966… rounds to 4.50; the unrounded value is 4.497 to 4 s.f.
ms:
M1 for 505 and 7.95 seen
M1 for √(505 ÷ (π × 7.95)) oe
A1 for 4.496… or 4.497 seen before rounding to 4.50
